## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t6-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Cheap energy</dt><dd>Fill the year with many MWh at a low running cost; capacity factor times the year's hours gives the MWh per MW, running cost (lesson 7) the rest.</dd>
<dt>Firm capacity</dt><dd>Be there in the riskiest hours; firm share rates it, as planning credit rather than a promise for any hour.</dd>
<dt>Flexibility</dt><dd>Change output quickly on request; <span class="lx-term" data-term="ramp-rate">ramp rate</span> and start-up time measure it.</dd>
<dt>Two different numbers</dt><dd>Gas peakers averaged 13.6% of their size in 2025, yet PJM credits 67% of their MW toward reliability; solar averaged 24.0% but is credited 7%.</dd>
<dt>No single winner</dt><dd>No technology does all three jobs best, so grids combine them.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>How a grid measures firm share</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A [firm share]{.lx-term term="firm-share"}, which PJM calls an ELCC class rating, asks: how much steady, always-available capacity would keep the grid exactly as reliable as this plant does?

Planners answer it by simulating many weather years with random plant outages.

- **It depends on the grid.** The numbers here are PJM's for its 2028/29 auction; another region, or another year, gives others.
- **It falls as more of the same is added.** The tenth solar farm shifts the riskiest hours into the evening, so it counts for less than the first, though not always.
- **Longer storage counts more.** PJM counts 59% of a 4-hour battery's MW, 68% at 6 hours, 71% at 8 and 78% at 10.
- **Classes, not plants.** These are ratings for technology classes; PJM can accredit a single plant differently.

Analyst lesson [A5](a05-adequacy.qmd) runs this simulation for the Plains grid.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The three jobs as three kinds of rule in a planning model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A planning model turns the three jobs into rules. In words:

- **Decisions.** How many MW of each technology to build, and how much each one makes every hour.
- **Goal.** The lowest total cost of building and running them.
- **Rule 1, energy.** Supply equals demand in every hour.
- **Rule 2, firm capacity.** The firm MW add up to the year's peak demand plus a safety margin.
- **Rule 3, flexibility.** No plant changes its output faster than its ramp limit.

Rule 2 in symbols: $C_g$ is the MW of technology $g$, $f_g$ its firm share, $\sum_g$ adds over every technology, $D_\text{peak}$ is the year's peak demand and $m$ the safety margin (an illustrative planning choice, for example 0.15):

$$
\textstyle\sum_g f_g\, C_g \;\ge\; (1 + m)\, D_\text{peak}
$$

[Lesson 10](10-write-it-down.qmd) teaches how to write rules like these down; [lesson 13](13-capstone.qmd) asks a solver for Prairie Town's least-cost mix.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t6-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cfirm" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plant's capacity factor tells you how much it counts toward the grid's reliability needs.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Solar's capacity factor was 24.0% in 2025, but PJM credits 7% of its MW toward reliability; gas peakers averaged 13.6% but are credited 67%.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="battery" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A battery is a source of energy.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It moves energy in time and loses some on the way: the U.S. battery fleet gave back 82% of what it stored (2019 data).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="idle" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A gas peaker with a capacity factor of only 13.6% is not doing a useful job.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A gas peaker's job is to be there at the peak and to move fast; whether that is the best way to do the job is a question of cost (lesson 7).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t6">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="measure" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Two plants have the same size in MW. Which number tells you which one a grid credits with more <span class="lx-term" data-term="firm-capacity">firm capacity</span>?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Its capacity factor</li><li data-value="b">Its firm share</li><li data-value="c">Its start-up time</li><li data-value="d">Its running cost</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Its firm share: at equal size, the higher share means more MW credited. For plants of different sizes, compare size × firm share.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="flexjob" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which job does a 4-hour battery do best?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Cheap energy</li><li data-value="b">Firm capacity, for as long as any peak lasts</li><li data-value="c">Flexibility</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Flexibility: it switches between charging and discharging almost at once. It helps with firm capacity only for as long as its stored energy lasts (PJM's 4-hour rating: 59%).</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<p>Regions reward these services differently: through energy prices, <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-market">capacity payments</span> or planning requirements, and payments for <span class="lx-term" data-term="reserves">reserves</span> and fast response. Which technology wins each depends on the region's rules and weather.</p>

<ul>
<li>EIA. Electric Power Monthly, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_6_07_a">Table 6.07.A</a> and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_6_07_b">Table 6.07.B</a>: capacity factors of U.S. utility-scale generators. Data for August 2026, released 23 October 2026.</li>
<li>PJM (2026). <a href="https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/planning/res-adeq/elcc/28-29-bra-elcc-class-ratings.pdf">ELCC Class Ratings for the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction</a> (PDF).</li>
<li>EIA (2021). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=46756">Utility-scale batteries and pumped storage return about 80% of the electricity they store</a>. Today in Energy.</li>
<li>NREL (2019). <a href="https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy19osti/73866.pdf">Grid-Friendly Renewable Energy: Solar and Wind Participation in Automatic Generation Control Systems</a>: wind and solar held below their available output can raise it on request.</li>
<li>FERC staff (2025). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/25_Annual%20Assessment%20of%20Demand%20Response_1212.pdf">2025 Assessment of Demand Response and Advanced Metering</a> (PDF).</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930): the Southwest Power Pool's 2025 wind data behind the calm spell.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
